description: Our project is a web tool for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It compares the Sun and Earth elevation at lunar south pole landing sites over a chosen date range. Planners can see when a site has sunlight, when it has a direct line to Earth, and when it has both, and how much time remains before sunset or Earthset. We check our results against JPL Horizons.
summary: Earthset is a web tool that compares lunar landing sites by the two things that shape a south pole mission: sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communication. A user picks from 19 sites or enters coordinates, sets a landing date and a window of up to 60 days, and gets Good, Medium or Poor verdicts for solar power, the Earth link, and both at once. The tool shows countdowns to when power or the link ends or returns, elevation plots, and an animated sky view that plays through time. A delay option (+1, +3 or +7 days) shows how a schedule slip changes the verdicts and where the Sun and Earth would be. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons. This version assumes a smooth Moon with no terrain, so results show the best case.
details:
What it does: Earthset compares lunar landing sites by sunlight for power and line of sight to Earth for communication. It is built for mission planners, educators and the public.

How it works: The user picks sites (19 are listed, plus custom coordinates), a landing date and a window of 1 to 60 days. Earthset requests hourly Sun and Earth elevation and compass direction from NASA JPL Horizons for an observer on the Moon's surface. It shows verdict cards, a comparison table with the longest dark spell and longest Earth-out spell, elevation plots with the usable periods shaded, countdowns to when power or the Earth link ends or returns, and an animated sky view with a time slider and a Play button. A line on each elevation plot moves with the animation. Users can set a minimum Sun and Earth elevation, and test a landing delay of 1, 3 or 7 days: empty rings in the sky view show where the Sun and Earth would be if the landing slips. Verdict thresholds (Good at 70% of the window or more, Medium from 30%, Poor below) are our own choice and are stated on the page.

What we noticed: At Malapert massif, Earth stays within a few degrees of due north, low on the horizon, while the Sun circles through every compass direction. The sky view shows this directly.

Checks and limits: We compared the elevation ranges with simple geometry. At about 86 degrees south the Sun stays below roughly 6 degrees, as expected from the Moon's 1.5 degree axial tilt. The tool assumes a smooth Moon with no terrain, so results show the best case. The app warns about this for sites south of 80 degrees south. Real horizons are shaped by mountains and crater walls, and adding LOLA terrain is the next step. Coordinates for Shackleton, Malapert massif, Connecting Ridge, Nobile and Haworth were read from Quickmap. Other site coordinates are approximate.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, astroquery, pandas, NumPy and Matplotlib, hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. Source code: https://github.com/souadbellagoune/earthset

A companion page by Melissa gives a fast two-site view: https://lunar-site-navigator.github.io/lunar-landing-site-navigator/ and also we work as a team .
